paras: The Chipley turpentine camp shooting was a night attack in early August 1900 in which about a dozen masked men fired into the quarters of a turpentine camp near Chipley, Washington County, Florida, whose occupants were mostly Black. One man was killed outright and four were wounded, two of whom were reported to have died later; a coroner's jury blamed unknown parties, and two farmers were jailed on suspicion. A Pensacola dispatch presented the shooting as the climax of a campaign to drive Black people out of the area, a picture the Chipley newspaper rejected as slander.

According to the Pensacola special, events in Washington County had been kept quiet in the hope that those responsible might be caught, and only then were made public. For some time before the attack, the dispatch said, "indiscriminate shooting and attempts to murder" had been of almost daily occurrence near Chipley, the county seat.

On a Thursday night, apparently August 2, about a dozen masked men went to the quarters of a turpentine camp, called the occupants out, and fired several volleys from Winchester rifles and shotguns into them. One Black man was killed instantly and four were dangerously wounded, two of whom were reported to have died on the following Monday morning. The rest ran back inside at the first volley and barred the doors and windows, and although the firing went on for several minutes no one else was hit.
Two days later, on Saturday morning, a disguised man confronted a white man at his post in the turpentine district, told him to "move on, and not come back," and fired shots at him.

A coroner's jury found that the dead man had died of gunshot wounds "inflicted by unknown parties." Two farmers were suspected and jailed, but the dispatch said the arrests had not quieted what it called the "lawless element." Turpentine operators were reported to be finding help hard to obtain and to be having trouble running their stills. No report of an indictment or trial of the two farmers appears in the coverage.

The story reached print as a special from Pensacola, first in the Florida column of the Savannah Morning News on August 9 under the heading "A Bad State of Affairs." The Dawson News of Georgia ran a fuller version on August 15 headlined "Are Afraid to Work. Reign of Terror in Florida Among Negroes," with a deck that put the wounded at three rather than the four given in its text. Its closing paragraph framed the violence as both a labor problem and a racial campaign, reporting that local whites were said to have "a deadly hatred for negroes" and to be determined to drive them away or "exterminate them altogether."

The same day, the Ocala Evening Star reported that F. C. Jones, editor of the Chipley Press, protested the way "the leading papers of the country" had slandered his town and insisted that Chipley was quiet and law abiding. Jones's protest, as summarized, did not address the camp shooting or the inquest, and the Star added only that his statement "makes Chipley all right." No coverage of the attack was found in the Black press.

The death toll rests partly on report: the dispatch said two of the wounded were "reported as having died," while the coroner's verdict it describes concerned a single dead man. The Pensacola account of near-daily violence around Chipley was contradicted in general terms by the town's own paper, which dismissed the reports without offering a different account of the shooting.

reader.title: Chipley turpentine camp shooting
bases: A band of about a dozen masked men fired on the mostly Black occupants of a turpentine camp at night amid a run of disguised attacks and warnings to 'move on' in the turpentine district, which the report tied to a reported white wish to drive Black people from the area (A2, A3).

One Black man was reported killed outright and two of four wounded reported dead later at the hands of about a dozen masked men acting without any authority (A2, A3); no accusation against the victims is reported, and the only motive given is the hearsay that local whites hated Black people and meant to drive them out or exterminate them (A3), so the racial pretext is reported but not established.

The shooting rests on a single Pensacola special printed in Savannah (A1, A2) and later in Dawson (A3), and the Chipley Press editor, as summarized in Ocala, denied that Chipley was lawless and called the coverage slander, without addressing the shooting itself (A4).

accounts.label: Pensacola special (wire report)
accounts.gist: About a dozen masked men fired into a turpentine camp's quarters near Chipley, killing one Black man and wounding four, two of whom reportedly died; a coroner's jury blamed unknown parties and two farmers were jailed; local whites were said to want Black people driven out or exterminated.

accounts.label: Chipley Press editor (as summarized by the Ocala Evening Star)
accounts.gist: Chipley is quiet and law abiding, and the leading papers' 'yellow covered accounts' slandered the town and its people.

framing.detail: The Pensacola special called it 'a terrible state of affairs' and a 'climax' of 'indiscriminate shooting and attempts to murder,' and Dawson headlined it 'REIGN OF TERROR IN FLORIDA AMONG NEGROES,' while also stressing the labor shortage.
The Ocala Evening Star relayed the Chipley Press denial without comment beyond 'Jones' statement makes Chipley all right.'
